---
title: "Redox and environmental cycles exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Nitrification acid demand

Oxidise 0.100 mmol/L NH₄⁺ completely to nitrate using the supplied reaction. Find O₂ demand and H⁺ production.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use the balanced coefficients 1:2:2.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
O₂ demand = **0.200 mmol/L** = **6.40 mg/L** using 32.0 mg/mmol. H⁺ production = **0.200 mmol/L**, corresponding to a **0.200 meq/L alkalinity decrease** in the stated net model.
:::

## 2. Denitrification donor

Reduce 0.0800 mmol/L nitrate entirely to N₂ with the CH₂O model. Find organic carbon consumption and N₂ production.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use five CH₂O and two N₂ for four nitrate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Carbon consumption = **0.100 mmol C/L** = **1.20 mg C/L** using 12.0 mg/mmol. N₂ production = **0.0400 mmol/L**. The carbon demand excludes biomass and alternative sinks.
:::

## 3. Check a half-reaction

Verify atoms and charge for FeOOH + 3 H⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ + 2 H₂O. What is reduced?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
FeOOH contains one hydrogen and two oxygens.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Both sides have 1 Fe, 2 O, and 4 H. Left charge is +3 − 1 = **+2**, matching right charge. Fe(III) gains one electron to become **Fe(II)**.
:::

## 4. An anoxic sediment observation

Dissolved iron and phosphate rise while oxygen declines above a sediment. Give a coupled explanation and one reason it is not proven by correlation alone.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The carrier phase can change oxidation state while phosphate retains its own oxidation state.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Organic-matter oxidation can consume O₂ and support reduction of Fe(III) solids; associated phosphate can be released. Mixing, other mineral changes, and independent sources could also produce patterns. Use Fe(II), solid-phase, porewater, and time/flux observations to test the explanation.
:::

## Explore: the electron-acceptor ladder {#explore}

Predict the order in which oxygen, nitrate, iron(III) oxide and sulfate are
used up as organic matter decomposes in a closed bottom water. When does
phosphate first appear?

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="redox" role="group" aria-label="Electron acceptors used as organic matter decomposes">
<p>Reference case: 0.500 mmol C/L decomposed uses up 0.30 mmol/L O₂, 0.080 mmol/L nitrate and 0.20 mmol/L Fe(III) oxide, releasing 0.020 mmol/L phosphate and reducing 0.025 mmol/L sulfate.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/redox.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Denitrification worked example**. Check the carbon used and
the N₂ formed against exercise 2.

**E2.** Choose **Oxygen still present**, then slowly raise the organic matter.
At what amount of carbon is phosphate first released? Explain why the
phosphate waits for oxygen and nitrate to run out, although phosphorus is
never reduced.

**E3.** In **Baltic bottom water**, why does 2.00 mmol/L sulfate last so much
longer than 0.20 mmol/L iron oxide? Use both the amounts and the electrons per
acceptor. Then choose **Low-sulfate lake water**: what forms once sulfate is
gone?

### Model conditions and hand check

Each CH₂O carbon gives 4 electrons when it is oxidised to CO₂. O₂ takes 4
electrons, nitrate (to N₂) 5, Fe(III) (to Fe²⁺) 1 and sulfate (to HS⁻) 8.
So the carbon needed is 1 mol C per mol O₂, 1.25 per mol nitrate, 0.25 per
mol Fe(III) and 2 per mol sulfate. In the reference case, oxygen uses
**0.300 mmol C/L**, nitrate **0.100**, and the iron oxide **0.050**, a total
of 0.450 mmol C/L. The remaining 0.050 mmol C/L reduces **0.025 mmol/L
sulfate**. For exercise 2, 0.0800 mmol/L nitrate needs **0.100 mmol C/L**
(1.20 mg C/L) and gives **0.0400 mmol/L N₂**.

The starting amounts are constructed, per litre of bottom water, with the
reactive iron oxide at the sediment surface counted in the same litre.
The phosphate held on the oxide is set at 0.1 mol P per mol Fe and is all
released as the oxide is reduced; none is sorbed again. Acceptors are used
strictly in order. Manganese oxides, biomass growth, intermediates such as
nitrite, and FeS formation are left out. Organic matter left after sulfate
is gone forms CO₂ and methane (2 CH₂O → CO₂ + CH₄). Real sediments overlap
the steps in space and time.
